definition: The water a field gives back to the air in two ways: evaporation from wet soil, crop residue and wet leaves, and transpiration, the water a plant takes up through its roots and releases to the air from its leaves.
here: The tool uses it in two forms: reference evapotranspiration and potential water demand.
source: K-State, Efficient Crop Water Use in Kansas (MF3066, August 2012), Chapter 3, Crop Water Use: "The term evapotranspiration is the combination of two terms: evaporation and transpiration", followed by a sentence that defines each. https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/MF3066.pdf

definition: The evapotranspiration from a reference surface that is not short of water: a hypothetical grass crop with specific characteristics.
here: The tool works it out for each day from NASA POWER weather (temperature, sunlight, humidity and wind), the place's latitude and the elevation NASA POWER gives for its grid cell, with the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation.
source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Allen, Pereira, Raes and Smith, 1998), Chapter 1, Reference crop evapotranspiration (ETo): "The evapotranspiration rate from a reference surface, not short of water, is called the reference crop evapotranspiration or reference evapotranspiration and is denoted as ETo. The reference surface is a hypothetical grass reference crop with specific characteristics." https://www.fao.org/4/X0490E/x0490e04.htm

definition: A ratio found by experiment: a crop's evapotranspiration under standard conditions divided by reference evapotranspiration. Reference ET times the crop coefficient gives the figure for that crop.
here: The tool uses the FAO-56 values for the start, the middle and the end of each crop's season.
source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Allen, Pereira, Raes and Smith, 1998), Chapter 1: "Experimentally determined ratios of ETc/ETo, called crop coefficients (Kc), are used to relate ETc to ETo or ETc = Kc ETo." https://www.fao.org/4/X0490E/x0490e04.htm

definition: The tool's name for what FAO-56 calls crop evapotranspiration under standard conditions: the evapotranspiration of a disease-free, well-fertilized crop in a large field, with the best soil water conditions, reaching full production in the given climate.
here: Worked out from the average reference ET of each month over the last {recentYears} years, times the crop coefficient for each day, added up over the crop's usual Kansas season.
note: FAO-56 discourages calling reference evapotranspiration potential ET, because the word has been defined in more than one way. It says nothing of the kind about crop demand: carrying the caution over is this tool's own care. The tool uses potential only in the plain sense of what a crop would use if water were never short, and means the quantity defined here, estimated as described above.
source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Allen, Pereira, Raes and Smith, 1998), Chapter 1, Crop evapotranspiration under standard conditions (ETc): "The crop evapotranspiration under standard conditions, denoted as ETc, is the evapotranspiration from disease-free, well-fertilized crops, grown in large fields, under optimum soil water conditions, and achieving full production under the given climatic conditions." Under its heading Reference crop evapotranspiration (ETo), the same chapter says: "The use of other denominations such as potential ET is strongly discouraged due to ambiguities in their definitions." https://www.fao.org/4/X0490E/x0490e04.htm

definition: An account of the water coming into a field and the water leaving it. Rain and irrigation add water. Evaporation, the crop's own use (transpiration), drainage down through the soil and runoff are losses.
here: Water fit is a simple one: the usable part of the rain in a crop's season, plus water stored in the soil before planting, set against the crop's potential water demand.
source: K-State, Efficient Crop Water Use in Kansas (MF3066, August 2012), Chapter 2, Water Budget: "Precipitation and irrigation are additions to the cycle. Evaporation, caused by the sun and wind; transpiration, water used by the crop; drainage through the soil profile; and runoff are losses". https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/MF3066.pdf

definition: A common practice in the western Great Plains, with the goal of storing water in the soil for future crops.
here: In this tool, a year of a rotation in which nothing is planted is a fallow year. On the field calendar, a month in which no crop is in the ground for at least half of it is shown as bare.
source: K-State, Efficient Crop Water Use in Kansas (MF3066, August 2012), Chapter 2, Fallow and Water Storage: "Fallow is a common practice in the western Great Plains, with the goal being to store water in the soil profile for future crops." https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/MF3066.pdf

definition: In this tool, a rotation scored on rain and stored soil water alone, with no irrigation.
The mix of sand, silt and clay in a soil, named in standard USDA terms. Loam, for example, is 7 to 27 percent clay, 28 to 50 percent silt and less than 52 percent sand.
here: The figure is for the surface layer of the map unit's main soil. No score uses it.
source: USDA NRCS Soil Data Access, the soil survey's own description of "Surface Texture" (table sdvattribute, read 2026-11-14): "Texture is given in the standard terms used by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. These terms are defined according to percentages of sand, silt, and clay in the fraction of the soil that is less than 2 millimeters in diameter." It gives loam as 7 to 27 percent clay, 28 to 50 percent silt, and less than 52 percent sand. https://sdmdataaccess.sc.egov.usda.gov/Query.aspx

definition: The water a soil can hold for plants: the amount held between field capacity, which is what stays in the soil once the excess has drained away, and the wilting point, where plants can no longer take the remaining water out.
here: The figure shown is the soil survey's available water supply for the top 100 cm (39 in) of the map unit, which the survey works out from each layer's available water capacity and thickness. The tool uses it as the most water the soil can store for the next crop.
sourceName: USDA NRCS soil survey and K-State MF3066
source: USDA NRCS Soil Data Access, the soil survey's own description of "Available Water Supply, 0 to 100 cm" (table sdvattribute, read 2026-11-14): "It is commonly estimated as the amount of water held between field capacity and the wilting point, with corrections for salinity, rock fragments, and rooting depth." and "AWS is calculated as the available water capacity times the thickness of each soil horizon to a specified depth." https://sdmdataaccess.sc.egov.usda.gov/Query.aspx ; K-State, Efficient Crop Water Use in Kansas (MF3066, August 2012), Chapter 2: "Field capacity refers to the amount of water that is stored in the soil after the excess (gravitational) water has drained away", and at the permanent wilting point "plants are not able to extract this water". https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/MF3066.pdf

definition: Plant and animal residue in the soil at various stages of decomposition, given as a percentage, by weight, of the soil material finer than 2 millimeters.
here: The figure is for the surface layer of the map unit's main soil. No score uses it.
source: USDA NRCS Soil Data Access, the soil survey's own description of "Organic Matter" (table sdvattribute, read 2026-11-14): "Organic matter is the plant and animal residue in the soil at various stages of decomposition. The estimated content of organic matter is expressed as a percentage, by weight, of the soil material that is less than 2 millimeters in diameter." https://sdmdataaccess.sc.egov.usda.gov/Query.aspx

definition: The difference in height between two points, as a percentage of the distance between them.
here: The figure is the soil survey's slope for the whole map unit (its column slopegradwta). The tool multiplies it by the K factor to rate the risk of erosion by water.
note: No description of that column was found. At the one map unit that was checked, it matched the average of the soils' slopes weighted by each soil's share of the unit.
source: USDA NRCS Soil Data Access, the soil survey's own description of "Representative Slope" (table sdvattribute, read 2026-11-14): "Slope gradient is the difference in elevation between two points, expressed as a percentage of the distance between those points." https://sdmdataaccess.sc.egov.usda.gov/Query.aspx

definition: How easily water erodes a soil, by what the soil survey calls sheet and rill erosion. Values run from 0.02 to 0.69. Other things being equal, the higher the value, the more easily the soil erodes.
here: The tool multiplies it by the slope to rate the risk of erosion by water.
source: USDA NRCS Soil Data Access, the soil survey's own description of "K Factor, Whole Soil" (table sdvattribute, read 2026-11-14): "Erosion factor K indicates the susceptibility of a soil to sheet and rill erosion by water." and "Values of K range from 0.02 to 0.69. Other factors being equal, the higher the value, the more susceptible the soil is to sheet and rill erosion by water." https://sdmdataaccess.sc.egov.usda.gov/Query.aspx

definition: How easily wind erodes a soil, given as the tons per acre per year that can be expected to be lost to wind erosion. Wind erosion is closely related to the texture of the surface layer, among other things.
here: The tool rates the risk of erosion by wind from it.
source: USDA NRCS Soil Data Access, the soil survey's own description of "Wind Erodibility Index" (table sdvattribute, read 2026-11-14): "The wind erodibility index is a numerical value indicating the susceptibility of soil to wind erosion, or the tons per acre per year that can be expected to be lost to wind erosion. There is a close correlation between wind erosion and the texture of the surface layer, the size and durability of surface clods, rock fragments, organic matter, and a calcareous reaction." https://sdmdataaccess.sc.egov.usda.gov/Query.aspx

definition: A letter from A to D for how fast a bare, thoroughly wet soil takes in water during a long storm, and so how much runs off. Group A takes water in fast and has low runoff potential. Group D takes it in very slowly and has high runoff potential. In a pair such as B/D, the first letter is for drained areas and the second for undrained ones.
here: Shown as a soil fact. No score uses it.
source: USDA NRCS Soil Data Access, the soil survey's own description of "Hydrologic Soil Group" (table sdvattribute, read 2026-11-14): "Soils are assigned to one of four groups according to the rate of water infiltration when the soils are not protected by vegetation, are thoroughly wet, and receive precipitation from long-duration storms." https://sdmdataaccess.sc.egov.usda.gov/Query.aspx

definition: The tool's rating, from 0 to 100, of how easily this soil erodes. It is the higher of two ratings: by water, the K factor times the slope in percent, highest at {kTimesSlopeCap} or more; and by wind, the wind erodibility index, highest at {windIndexCap} or more.
A day whose high in NASA POWER is {hotDayF}°F or above. The threshold is the tool's choice.
Rain from {growingSeason}, added up for each year. The months are the tool's own choice of growing season.
The National Weather Service uses the word when the surface air temperature is expected to be 32°F or below over a widespread area for a climatologically significant period of time.
here: In this tool, a freeze day is a day whose low in NASA POWER is {freezeF}°F or below. The last one from January to June is the last spring freeze, and the first one from July to December is the first fall freeze.
source: U.S. National Weather Service, Glossary, Freeze: "when the surface air temperature is expected to be 32°F or below over a widespread area for a climatologically significant period of time". https://forecast.weather.gov/glossary.php?word=freeze

definition: A month in which a day of {hotDayF}°F or above occurred in more than half of the last {recentYears} years on record. The rule is the tool's own, and no score uses it.

A month in which reference evapotranspiration runs further ahead of rain than it does in this field's average month, on the last {recentYears} years on record. The rule is the tool's own, and no score uses it.

The months from the average first fall freeze to the average last spring freeze at this place, over every year on record that had one. A crop in the ground in those months can meet a freeze. The rule is the tool's own, and no score uses it.

The label on each climate chart. Likely trend: the Mann-Kendall test gives a p-value below {likelyBelowP}. Possible trend: from {likelyBelowP} to {possibleUpToP}. No clear trend: above {possibleUpToP}. The cut-offs are the tool's own.

A test for whether a series of values is rising or falling over time. It takes every pair of years and counts the pairs that rose against the pairs that fell: a large surplus either way is evidence of a trend. It does not assume the values follow any particular distribution.
here: The tool runs it on each yearly series since 1981 and reports a two-sided p-value, because it does not know the direction in advance.
source: U.S. EPA, Guidance for Data Quality Assessment: Practical Methods for Data Analysis (EPA QA/G-9, QA00 update, July 2000), sections 4.3.4 and 4.3.4.1: "The Mann-Kendall test does not assume any particular distributional form" and "The Mann-Kendall test involves computing a statistic S, which is the difference between the number of pairwise slopes (described in 4.3.3.1) that are positive minus the number that are negative." https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-06/documents/g9-final.pdf

definition: The probability of seeing a result at least as extreme as the one found if there were in fact no trend. The smaller it is, the stronger the evidence of a trend.
here: The tool calls a trend likely when p is below {likelyBelowP}, possible from {likelyBelowP} to {possibleUpToP}, and otherwise says there is no clear trend.
source: U.S. EPA, Guidance for Data Quality Assessment: Practical Methods for Data Analysis (EPA QA/G-9, QA00 update, July 2000), section 5.2.1: the p-value "is defined as the probability, assuming the null hypothesis to be true, of observing a test result at least as extreme as that found in the sample". Section 4.3.4.1 gives the null hypothesis of the Mann-Kendall test: "that there is no temporal trend in the data values". https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-06/documents/g9-final.pdf

definition: An estimate of how fast a series is changing. The slope between every pair of years is worked out and the middle one, the median, is taken. That makes it insensitive to outliers, such as one extreme year.
here: The tool reports it as the change per decade.
source: U.S. EPA, Guidance for Data Quality Assessment: Practical Methods for Data Analysis (EPA QA/G-9, QA00 update, July 2000), section 4.3.3.1: "This approach involves computing slopes for all the pairs of ordinal time points and then using the median of these slopes as an estimate of the overall slope. As such, it is insensitive to outliers". https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-06/documents/g9-final.pdf

definition: The slope of the straight line that best fits all the values at once. Regression is very sensitive to extreme values (outliers), and it relies on errors that are normally distributed with a constant variance.
here: The tool fits the line by ordinary least squares. It works the slope out only to set it beside Sen's slope on the About the data tab.
source: U.S. EPA, Guidance for Data Quality Assessment: Practical Methods for Data Analysis (EPA QA/G-9, QA00 update, July 2000), section 4.3.2.1: "Regression is very sensitive to extreme values (outliers)", and it "relies on two key assumptions: normally distributed errors, and constant variance". https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-06/documents/g9-final.pdf

definition: A measure, made from space, of how densely green a patch of land is: the near-infrared light it reflects minus the visible light, divided by the two added together. It runs from -1 to +1. No green leaves gives a value close to zero, and a value close to +1 (0.8 to 0.9) means the highest possible density of green leaves.
here: The map layer shows it in {vegetationPeriod} pictures, from the MODIS instrument on NASA's Terra satellite, at {vegetationResolution} to a reading at its sharpest. Readings of zero or below are left clear. It is a picture only: no score uses it.
source: NASA Earth Observatory, Measuring Vegetation (NDVI & EVI), 30 August 2000 (page last updated 14 November 2025): "near-infrared radiation minus visible radiation divided by near-infrared radiation plus visible radiation. The result of this formula is called the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)." and "Calculations of NDVI for a given pixel always result in a number that ranges from minus one (-1) to plus one (+1); however, no green leaves gives a value close to zero. A zero means no vegetation and close to +1 (0.8 - 0.9) indicates the highest possible density of green leaves." https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/measuring-vegetation-ndvi-evi/

definition: How much of the crops' potential water demand is covered at this field. On rain alone, it is the share covered by the usable part of the rain in each crop's season plus the water stored in the soil before planting, averaged over the crops. On an irrigated field it is the lower of that and a score that falls as the pumping needed rises, reaching 0 at {irrigationNeedCapIn} in a year.

Higher is safer. The score falls as the days at or above {hotDayF}°F in each crop's heat-sensitive month rise, on the average of the last {recentYears} years, and reaches 0 at {hotDaysCap} such days in that month. Where the yearly count of hot days is likely rising, {risingTrendPenalty} points are taken off. Drought itself is scored under water fit.
Starts at 100 and loses points in proportion to the share of months the field is bare and to the erosion risk of this soil. A field that is bare half the time on the most erodible soil scores 50.
{nFixing} points for a nitrogen-fixing crop, {highResidue} for a high-residue crop, {coverCrop} for a cover crop and {deepRoots} for a deep-rooted crop.
Rises with the number of different crops and falls with the longest run of years in which the same crop is planted. The same crop every year scores 0. The formula is the tool's own.

The average over the crops that are sold: {marketLocal} for a crop a local elevator takes, {marketRegional} for one that needs a regional buyer, {marketContract} for one grown only on contract. Which crop needs which is a tool assumption.

100 for a single crop, less {perExtraCrop} for each further crop to manage, and less {missingNoTillPenalty} when the rotation needs no-till equipment the farm does not have. The score cannot go below 0.
